results.ask: What's the duty cycle for MIG welding at 200A on 240V?
results.text: 25% duty cycle at 200A/240V MIG: 2.5 minutes welding, 7.5 minutes resting per 10-minute period [p.7, p.19].

results.tests: diagnosis from the troubleshooting matrix, with the weld photo
results.ask: My flux-cored welds have porosity. What should I check?
results.text:
Since flux-cored is gasless, ignore the gas-related causes in the porosity list — those apply to MIG only. For flux-cored specifically, check these:

1. **Polarity** — Flux-cored (self-shielded, no gas) must be set to **DCEN** (electrode negative): ground clamp in **positive** socket, wire feed power cable in **negative** socket. Wrong polarity is the #1 named cause of porosity [p.43].
2. **Dirty workpiece or wire** — clean workpiece to bare metal; make sure wire is free of rust, oil, or coatings [p.37].
3. **Inconsistent travel speed** — keep a steady pace [p.37].
4. **CTWD too long** — keep contact tip within 1/2" of the work [p.37].Start with polarity — it's the easiest thing to get backwards and matches your symptom exactly.

results.ask: How do I set polarity for flux-cored? Which socket does the ground clamp go in?
results.text:
Flux-cored (gasless) runs **DCEN** (direct current, electrode negative):

- **Ground clamp cable → Positive (+) socket**
- **Wire feed power cable → Negative (–) socket**

Twist both cables clockwise until they lock in place [p.13].

This is the opposite of solid-wire MIG (which is DCEP, ground in negative). If you're switching between flux-cored and gas-shielded solid wire on the same machine, double check you've swapped both cables, not just one.Also loosen the Knob on the wire feed mechanism to insert the gun cable connector, and make sure it's pushed in fully — a partially seated connector will leak the gas fitting even though flux-cored doesn't use shielding gas, since it can still cause a poor electrical connection [p.13].

results.tests: refusing cleanly on something the manuals never cover
results.ask: Can I run this welder off a portable generator? What size generator do I need?
results.text:
The manual doesn't cover generator use at all — no section addresses portable generators, and I'm not able to state a generator wattage size since that number isn't printed anywhere in the manual. Giving you a made-up figure would be worse than no answer.

What the manual does specify is input power draw, which is the number you'd hand to anyone calculating generator sizing:

- **120 VAC:** up to 20.8 A input (at 100 A MIG output) [p.7]
- **240 VAC:** up to 25.5 A input (at 200 A MIG output) [p.7]

It also requires a grounded, GFCI-protected outlet on a circuit with delayed-action circuit breakers or fuses [p.16], and explicitly says **do not use outdoors** [p.4] and **do not use an extension cord** [p.6] — both relevant if your generator plan involves running it outside or through a long cord to reach the garage.

If you're set on generator power, I'd suggest sizing based on that input current draw (amps × volts = watts, plus surge headroom) and checking with the generator manufacturer, since the welder manual gives no guidance of its own here.

results.tests: two sections combined: the 120V duty cycle and the flux-cored polarity
results.ask: I'm running flux-cored on 120V at 100A. How long can I weld before resting, and which socket does my ground clamp go in?
results.text:
**Duty cycle:** At 100A on 120V, flux-cored is rated 40% — 4 minutes welding, then 6 minutes resting, per 10-minute period [p.7, p.19].

**Ground clamp:** Flux-cored runs DCEN (electrode negative). Ground clamp goes in the **positive (+) socket**, and the wire feed power cable goes in the negative (–) socket [p.13].Twist both cables clockwise until they lock [p.13]. If you push past the 4-minute mark, the machine will thermally shut down and show a warning screen on the LCD until it cools — that's normal, not a fault [p.19].

results.tests: a setup answer that refuses to invent the two numbers the manual omits
results.ask: I want to weld 18 gauge steel with flux-cored wire on 120V. How do I set the machine up?
results.text:
A few things the configurator doesn't cover:

- Flux-cored runs DCEN (electrode negative) — ground clamp goes to the **positive** socket, wire feed power cable to **negative** [p.13]. Don't mix this up with solid-wire MIG, which is the opposite polarity.
- No shielding gas needed for flux-cored — it's self-shielded [p.18].
- Feed tensioner should be set to 2–3 for flux-cored wire (lower than solid wire) — over-tightening will crush it [p.15].
- Gun angle: tilt 0–15° in the direction of travel (drag angle), not push angle like solid wire [p.22].

Once you've got wire loaded and cables connected, the machine's auto weld settings will set wire feed speed/voltage for you based on the wire diameter and 18 gauge thickness you dial in on the front panel.

results.ask: Show me the wiring schematic for this welder.
results.text:
The full wiring schematic is on page 45 of the manual — it covers the AC input, power inverter stage, control boards, and feeder/solenoid wiring all on one diagram.That's the complete wiring schematic [p.45]. It runs left to right in stages:

- **AC input** (bottom left): AC1/AC2/ground terminals into the K1 switch, EMI filter, and thermal cutout (-T).
- **Power stage** (center): PFC and IGBT inverter feeding transformer T1, then the output rectifier bank up to the OUT+ / OUT- studs, with a Hall sensor on the output for current feedback.
- **MCU board and LCD screen** (upper right): the control brain, connected to the display via a ribbon cable at CN pins.
- **Remote board / feeder circuit** (lower right): wire feeder motor (M), solenoid valves (gas control), the fast wire feed switch, and the two aviation plug sockets on the front panel.
- **Cooling**: FAN and FAN2 driven off the 24V rail at bottom.

This is meant for a qualified technician diagnosing internal faults, not for routine setup — for that, the maintenance section on page 41 and the troubleshooting tables are the better reference. Anything you're trying to trace on here specifically?

results.tests: asking for the one missing fact instead of guessing it
results.ask: What's my duty cycle at 150 amps?
results.text:
I need a bit more info to look that up correctly:

1. **Which process** — MIG, TIG, or Stick?
2. **Which input voltage** — 120V or 240V?

150 A is above the 120V range for all three processes (MIG tops out at 140A, TIG at 125A, Stick at 80A on 120V) [p.7], so if you're on 120V, 150A isn't reachable at all — you'd need 240V.

Let me pull up the calculator so you can check once you confirm — I'll assume MIG at 240V as a starting point, but tell me if that's wrong.For **MIG at 240V**, the manual doesn't publish a duty cycle at exactly 150A — it only rates two points: 100% @ 115A and 25% @ 200A [p.7]. Duty cycle isn't linear, so there's no safe way to interpolate a number for 150A. Treat 115A as your continuous-safe current, and 200A as the 25%-duty (2.5 min on / 7.5 min off) current.If you're actually asking about **TIG or Stick**, or you're on **120V**, let me know and I'll pull the correct figures — those all have different amp ranges and none of them reach 150A on a 120V circuit.
